source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Aurora campus publishes 114 megawatts of IT capacity, which is 48 percent of all the data center power Illinois has disclosed.

Illinois has 44 mapped data center facilities and only six with published power figures. That ratio is the real finding: the state's disclosed capacity is mostly one campus plus a handful of others, and the remaining 38 facilities are invisible in power terms. At 40 kilowatts per rack, a common AI training density, 114 megawatts works out to roughly 2,850 racks, though the operator published no rack count. The 450,000 square feet yields about 6.3 megawatts per 10,000 square feet, which is typical of hyperscale colocation built in the last decade rather than a purpose-built accelerator hall.

For AI, the megawatt figure is the input that matters, because it sets the ceiling on how much compute the site can host. The published specifications stop at that ceiling. There is no power delivery tier, no redundancy topology, no cooling technology, and no cooling source. At 40 kilowatts per rack the thermal question is the binding one, and nothing in the record answers it.

The data also omits total campus power draw, PUE, renewable sourcing, grid connection characteristics, and interconnect uplinks to cloud regions. So the 48 percent share describes disclosed capacity, not installed capacity, and it says nothing about whether the local grid constrains the campus or whether it can move training data fast enough to be useful. Green Globes certification is the only environmental fact given, and it speaks to building performance, not to power supply.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
